points.title: Percentage change
points.brief: Percentage change shows how much something grew or fell compared with where it started, found by dividing the change by the starting value and multiplying by 100.

points.title: Predicting consumer and financial impacts
points.brief: Use a trend and what causes it to predict effects on people, such as rising interest rates making loan repayments larger.

points.title: Deciding with criteria
points.brief: Set criteria that matter, such as cost, risk and fairness, score each option against them, and choose the one that does best overall.

points.title: Building an argument with evidence
points.brief: An argument states a position, gives reasons, supports each with evidence from named sources, and answers the main view against it.

points.title: Financial institutions
points.brief: Banks, credit unions and building societies take deposits, keep money safe, make payments and lend to people and businesses.

points.title: How banks lend savings
points.brief: Banks pool many people's savings and lend them to borrowers, paying savers interest and charging borrowers a higher rate to make a profit.

points.title: What shapes the financial sector
points.brief: The financial sector changes with deregulation, new technology such as online banking, and how confident people and businesses feel about the future.

points.title: Finance for global business
points.brief: The financial sector helps businesses trade overseas by changing currencies, moving payments between countries, insuring goods and lending money.

points.title: Ways to invest
points.brief: People invest for future income through shares, term deposits, managed funds, property and superannuation.

points.title: Risk and return
points.brief: Investments that can earn more, such as shares, usually carry more risk of losing money than safer ones such as term deposits.

points.title: Good debt and bad debt
points.brief: Good debt pays for something that grows in value or earns income, such as study or a home. Bad debt pays for things that lose value, often at high interest.

points.title: Managing debt
points.brief: Borrow only what you can repay, pay high-interest debts first and keep savings for emergencies, to avoid owing more than you can manage.

points.title: An interdependent economy
points.brief: Consumers, businesses, the financial sector and government rely on each other, so a decision by one affects the others.

points.title: Globalisation
points.brief: Globalisation is the growing links between countries through trade, investment, technology and the movement of people and ideas.

points.title: Global supply chains
points.brief: Transnational corporations design, make and sell products across many countries, which lowers costs but can be disrupted by events far away.

points.title: How one economy affects another
points.brief: When one country's economy slows, its people buy fewer imports, so countries that export to it lose sales and jobs.

points.title: Why countries trade
points.brief: Countries have different resources and skills, so they trade to sell what they have spare and buy what they cannot make as well or as cheaply.

points.title: Specialisation and the benefits of trade
points.brief: Trade lets countries specialise in what they do best, which raises production, incomes and choice, and builds ties between countries.

points.title: Exports and imports
points.brief: Exports are goods and services sold to other countries. Imports are those bought from other countries.

points.title: Composition and direction of trade
points.brief: The composition of trade is what a country buys and sells. The direction of trade is which countries it trades with.

points.title: Australia's trade with Asia
points.brief: Asia buys most of Australia's exports, such as iron ore, coal, gas and education. China, Japan, South Korea and India are major partners.

points.title: How Australia's trade has changed
points.brief: In the 1950s Britain was Australia's main trading partner and wool and wheat led its exports. Japan then took the lead, and now Asia, led by China, buys most, mainly minerals and energy.

points.title: What competitive advantage is
points.brief: A competitive advantage is something that makes customers choose a business over its rivals, which helps it win sales and profit.

points.title: Lower costs
points.brief: A business can gain an advantage by producing more cheaply, through research, efficient methods, local resources or outsourcing.

points.title: Differentiation
points.brief: A business can stand out with better quality, design, service or brand, made known through advertising and social media.

points.title: Working with others to compete
points.brief: Businesses can share promotion costs with others in their industry, work with government to export, and train skilled staff.

points.title: First Nations cultural and intellectual property
points.brief: First Nations businesses protect their cultural expressions, such as art, designs and stories, through licensing and copyright, which keeps control and gives them an edge.

points.title: Scams and identity theft
points.brief: Scams trick people into giving money or personal details, often by pretending to be a bank or a business. Identity theft uses stolen details to commit fraud.

points.title: Managing financial risk
points.brief: People manage risk by setting financial goals, having insurance and savings, and checking before sharing details or paying.

points.title: Consumer rewards
points.brief: Loyalty programs, interest on savings and returns on investments reward people, but loyalty schemes also collect data and encourage spending.

points.title: Ethical consumer decisions
points.brief: Ethical decisions think about effects on others and the environment, such as buying products made without child labour.

points.title: Corporate social responsibility
points.brief: Corporate social responsibility is a business acting for the good of workers, communities and the environment, not only for profit.
